question: What does Cyrus's decree allow, and what kind of help does it ask of the neighbors of those who will return?
The text says the LORD “stirred the spirit of Cyrus” to fulfill the word of Jeremiah: how does the book understand the relationship between God and a foreign king?
The verb עוּר (ur, “stir up”) appears for Cyrus and for those who go up to Jerusalem: what does the repetition suggest about the origin of the return?
Not everyone goes back, but everyone can help: what is your role when God moves others to a task?
Besides the families, what groups linked to worship appear in the list, and what problem arises with some who claim to be priests?
Why such care in recording the names, places and numbers of those who returned from captivity?
Some sons of כֹּהֵן (kohen, “priest”) cannot find their record: why did belonging to the priesthood depend so much on genealogy, and what does the governor decide?
The leaders gave “according to their ability”: how can this standard guide your generosity?
What do the returned exiles rebuild first, even before the foundations of the temple, and why do they do it in fear?
What link does the praise of this chapter have with David's ordinance and with the psalms that say “His loving devotion endures forever”?
The word תְּרוּעָה (teruah, “shout of joy, acclamation”) mingles with the weeping of the old men: what does each group see in the same foundation?
Weeping and joy mingle until they cannot be told apart: how do you live through new beginnings that recall what was lost?
What offer do the adversaries make to Zerubbabel, and what do they do after being refused?
What arguments does the letter to Artaxerxes use against Jerusalem, and why do they touch the king's interests?
From 4:8 the text switches to Aramaic, the language of Persian administration; the Aramaic verb בְּטֵל (betel, “stop, cease”) marks the end of the chapter: what stops, and by whose order?
The people are discouraged “throughout the reign of Cyrus” until Darius: how do you react when a good project is blocked for a long time?
Who leads the people to resume the work, and who works alongside the builders?
How do the elders present themselves to the governor, and how do they explain the destruction of the first temple?
The Aramaic text says “the eye of their God” was on the elders, with the word עַיִן (ayin, “eye”): what meaning does this image give to Tattenai's investigation?
The elders say “we are the servants of the God of heaven and earth”: how do you present yourself when you need to explain your faith to someone in authority?
What does the decree found in Ecbatana determine, and what does Darius add to it?
The verse cites the prophecy of Haggai and Zechariah and the decrees of three kings: how does the book bring together God's action and human decisions in the completion of the temple?
The Aramaic word טְעֵם (teem, “decree, order”) is repeated in the chapter: how many orders intersect here, and which is the last one cited in 6:14?
The dedication of the temple and the Passover are celebrated “with joy”: what do you do to mark the end of a long wait?
How is Ezra introduced by his genealogy and his role, and how long does the journey last?
What order is there between “study,” “practice” and “teach” in Ezra's resolve, and why does it matter?
Ezra is called a סֹפֵר (sofer, “scribe”) of the law of Moses: what does this title indicate about his work, beyond copying texts?
Ezra blesses God for something a king decided: in what decisions of others have you recognized the hand of God?
What group is missing from the caravan at the Ahava canal, and how does Ezra deal with the lack?
Why is Ezra ashamed to ask the king for an escort, and how is the fast linked to what he had said before?
The phrase “the hand of our God,” with יָד (yad, “hand”), runs through the chapter: at what moments does it appear, and what is it said to do?
Ezra weighs and records everything before and after the journey: what care do you take with what others have entrusted to you?
What news does Ezra receive, and what are his gestures until the time of the evening sacrifice?
Why does Ezra pray in the first person plural, speaking of “our iniquities,” if he himself did not commit the offense denounced?
The word פְּלֵיטָה (peletah, “remnant, those who escaped”) is repeated in the prayer: what does Ezra fear will happen to this remnant?
Ezra speaks of “a little relief” in bondage: where do you recognize small mercies in the midst of hard times?
Who proposes the solution to the problem of the marriages, and how do the people respond to Ezra?
How should we read today the decision to send away wives and children, comparing this chapter with texts such as Ruth or with what the Law said about foreigners?
The word נׇכְרִי (nokri, “foreign”) qualifies the women throughout the chapter: what does the book fear in this mixing, according to 9:1-2?
The people tremble in the rain and ask for time to settle the matter in order: how do you seek to correct mistakes without haste?
